title: Negligence is the breach of a legal duty to take care resulting in damage

content.overview: Negligence is the breach of a legal duty to take care resulting in damage. Established by proving Duty (Donoghue / Caparo), Breach (reasonable person standard), and Causation (Wagon Mound foreseeability). Supported by Res Ipsa Loquitur and governed in professions by the Bolam / Jacob Mathew standard.

content.study:
Topic at a glance
Negligence in tort is the breach of a legal duty to take care which results in actionable damage to the plaintiff. Unlike criminal negligence (which requires gross recklessness), civil negligence is measured objectively against the standard of the "reasonable man" (the vir bonus or bonus paterfamilias). It is founded upon three indispensable elements: (1) a legal duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, (2) breach of that legal duty by failing to achieve the requisite standard of care, and (3) consequential damage suffered by the plaintiff that is legally recognized and not too remote.

Jurisprudential roots & legislative purpose
Historically, common law provided remedies only for nominate, intentional trespasses. The modern independent tort of negligence emerged as an organic response of sociological jurisprudence to the risks spawned by industrialization, mechanization, and mass consumer production. As Lord Atkin famously recognized in Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562, liability for negligence arises from a universal duty of care rooted in the Christian moral command to "love thy neighbour," transformed into the legal canon: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour."
In Indian law, where tort law is uncodified, the principles of justice, equity, and good conscience govern. The legislative policy behind recognizing negligence across common law and specialized statutes (such as the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Consumer Protection Act, 2019) is to enforce social responsibility, deter hazardous carelessness, and provide civil restitution (restitutio in integrum) through unliquidated damages.

Meaning and concept
Winfield defines negligence as "the breach of a legal duty to take care which results in damage, undesired by the defendant to the plaintiff."
Alderson, B., in Blyth v. Birmingham Waterworks Co. (1856), provided the classic definition: "Negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do."
Crucially, carelessness in the air does not constitute a tort. A person may be grossly careless, but unless they owe a specific legal duty to the plaintiff, no action in negligence lies (Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.).

The three essential elements
1. Legal Duty of Care: The defendant must owe a recognized legal obligation to take care. Whether a duty exists is determined by:
   - The Atkinian Neighbour Principle: Persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation.
   - The Modern Caparo Three-Fold Test (Caparo Industries plc v. Dickman [1990]): (i) Foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff, (ii) Proximity of relationship between the parties, and (iii) Whether it is fair, just, and reasonable for the court to impose a duty.
2. Breach of Duty: Failure to exercise the standard of care expected of a reasonable person in the same circumstances. The standard is objective. Factors determining breach include:
   - Magnitude and likelihood of the risk (Bolton v. Stone — cricket ball hit out of ground once in 30 years; no breach).
   - Gravity of the potential injury (Paris v. Stepney Borough Council — higher duty owed to a one-eyed workman).
   - Cost and practicality of taking precautions (Latimer v. A.E.C. Ltd. — sawdust spread on flooded factory floor; reasonable steps taken).
   - Social utility of the defendant's conduct (Daborn v. Bath Tramways — left-hand drive ambulance in wartime).
3. Consequential Damage: The plaintiff must suffer recognized harm (physical injury, property damage, or financial loss consequential upon physical harm). Mere mental distress without recognized psychiatric illness is not actionable.
   - Causation in Fact: The "But-For" Test (sine qua non) — would the damage have occurred but for the defendant's breach?
   - Remoteness of Damage: The damage must not be too remote. The Privy Council in The Wagon Mound (No. 1) [1961] established that the defendant is liable only for damage of such a kind as was reasonably foreseeable, decisively rejecting the older "direct consequence" test of In re Polemis [1921].

The doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur
Normally, the burden of proving negligence lies on the plaintiff. However, where the accident is of such a nature that it would not occur in the ordinary course of things without negligence, the maxim Res Ipsa Loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") applies.
As laid down in Scott v. London & St. Katherine Docks Co. (1865), three conditions are required:
1. The instrumentality causing the accident was under the exclusive management and control of the defendant.
2. The accident is such as does not happen in the ordinary course of things if those who manage it use proper care.
3. There is absence of explanation by the defendant.
Operation: Res ipsa loquitur is a rule of evidence, not of substantive law. When established, it creates a rebuttable presumption of negligence, effectively shifting the evidential burden to the defendant to prove that the accident occurred without their fault (Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti [1966] — clock tower collapsed).

Medical negligence and the Bolam / Jacob Mathew test
In the law of professional negligence, a professional is not required to possess the highest expert skill. The standard is that of an ordinary competent practitioner exercising that art.
- The Bolam Test (Bolam v. Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957]): A doctor is not guilty of negligence if they acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art.
- Supreme Court Ruling in Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) 6 SCC 1: The Supreme Court held that simple lack of care or an error of judgment does not constitute negligence. For criminal liability under penal law (old IPC 304A / now BNS 106), gross negligence is mandatory; in civil tort, failure to exercise ordinary competence according to accepted medical standards suffices.

Procedural & forum anchors (Senior Counsel Reference)
- Competent Forum:
  1. Regular Civil Court (Civil Judge Junior or Senior Division, depending on pecuniary valuation).
  2. Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 for vehicular negligence.
  3. Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (District, State, or National) under Consumer Protection Act, 2019 where the negligence amounts to "deficiency in service" (including private medical treatment).
- Limitation Period:
  - Suits for compensation for tort: Schedule to Limitation Act, 1963 — Article 72 (suits for act done in pursuance of enactment: 1 year); Article 113 (residuary suits: 3 years from when right to sue accrues).
- Standard and Burden of Proof:
  - Standard: Preponderance of probabilities (civil standard, distinct from beyond reasonable doubt).
  - General Burden: On the plaintiff under Section 104 BSA (old s. 101 IEA) to prove duty, breach, and causation.
  - Reversal: Evidential burden shifts to defendant upon invocation of Res Ipsa Loquitur.

Adversarial courtroom submissions
- Plaintiff / Claimant Submissions:
  1. The defendant stood in close proximity and owed an inescapable duty of care.
  2. The risk was foreseeable and preventable by taking reasonable precautions.
  3. The breach directly caused the damage without any novus actus interveniens.
  4. Rely on Res Ipsa Loquitur if the mechanism was under defendant's sole control.
- Defendant / Tortfeasor Submissions:
  1. No duty of care existed towards an unforeseeable plaintiff.
  2. Reasonable precautions were taken; the event was an inevitable accident or Act of God (vis major).
  3. Contributory negligence: The plaintiff failed to take care of their own safety (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act principles; proportionate reduction of damages).
  4. Novus actus interveniens: An independent, conscious act of a third party severed the causal chain.

Exceptions & affirmative defences
- Volenti non fit injuria: Plaintiff voluntarily consented to the risk with full knowledge.
- Inevitable accident: Event that could not have been prevented by the exercise of ordinary care and foresight.
- Act of God (Vis Major): Extraordinary operation of natural forces that could not be anticipated or guarded against.
- Contributory Negligence: Mitigates damages in proportion to plaintiff's share of responsibility.

Current-law close
In Indian civil practice, plead the specific duty, detail the omission against the reasonable person standard, demonstrate proximate causation under the Wagon Mound test, and claim unliquidated damages calculated on restitutio in integrum.

examples.title: Example — actionable negligence
examples.body: A municipal corporation fails to place barricades or warning lights around a deep excavation made in a poorly lit public road. A motorcyclist travelling at a lawful speed falls into the trench and suffers spinal injuries. The corporation owed a duty of care to road users, breached it by failing to fence the hazard, and the physical harm was directly foreseeable. The corporation is liable in negligence.

examples.title: Example — section/tort not attracted (unforeseeable plaintiff)
examples.body: A railway guard helps a passenger board a moving train. A small, unmarked package wrapped in newspaper drops from the passenger’s arm onto the rails. The package secretly contains fireworks, which explode. The concussive blast knocks down heavy scales thirty feet away, injuring Mrs. Palsgraf. Held: The guard may have been careless to the boarding passenger, but owed no duty of care to Palsgraf because harm to her was completely unforeseeable (Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.).

examples.title: Example — Res Ipsa Loquitur applied
examples.body: A pedestrian walking peacefully past a multi-storey flour warehouse is struck on the head by a heavy barrel of flour falling from a second-floor window. The pedestrian cannot prove the precise internal slip by a warehouse worker. Held: Barrels do not roll out of upper windows in the ordinary course of business unless those in control are negligent. The doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur applies, shifting the burden to the warehouse to prove lack of negligence (Byrne v. Boadle).

hypotheticals.question: Is Dr. Ananya liable in the tort of negligence? How will the court apply the Bolam test and the Supreme Court guidelines in Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab?
hypotheticals.analysis: To establish professional medical negligence, the claimant must prove that Dr. Ananya breached the standard of a reasonably competent general surgeon. Under the Bolam test, a medical practitioner is not negligent merely because an alternative course of action or treatment was available, provided the procedure adopted was endorsed by a responsible and respectable body of medical opinion. In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court ruled that a doctor cannot be held liable for an honest error of judgment or an unfortunate surgical complication where ordinary professional competence was applied. Here, Dr. Ananya was confronted with sudden severe vascular adhesions during emergency surgery and adopted a recognized surgical technique. The occurrence of haemorrhage was attributable to unforeseen anatomical fragility rather than gross ignorance, recklessness, or departure from accepted medical practice.

distinctions.title: Negligence in Tort vs Criminal Negligence

rows.left: Failure to exercise reasonable care (objective ordinary prudent person)
rows.right: Gross negligence, culpable rashness, or utter disregard for human life

rows.left: Unliquidated damages (compensatory restitution to the victim)
rows.right: Punishment (imprisonment and fine paid to the State)

rows.left: Mental state irrelevant; objective breach alone is evaluated
rows.right: Culpable mental state (mens rea of rashness/recklessness) required

distinctions.title: Remoteness of Damage: Wagon Mound vs In re Polemis

rows.left: Reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage
rows.right: Direct consequence test (liable for all direct results, however unforeseeable)

rows.left: Fair and proportionate; liability bounded by reasonable foresight
rows.right: Imposed crushing, indefinite liability on defendants for freak consequences

misconceptions.trap: Believing that any careless act is actionable in tort.
misconceptions.correction: Carelessness in the abstract is not a tort. There must be a specific legal duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, a breach of that duty, and legally recognized consequential damage (Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.).

misconceptions.trap: Assuming Res Ipsa Loquitur is an independent cause of action or substantive tort.
misconceptions.correction: Res Ipsa Loquitur is merely a rule of evidence regarding circumstantial proof. It allows the court to draw a rebuttable inference of negligence, shifting the evidential burden to the defendant without altering the substantive tort of negligence.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Define negligence as a tort. Explain its essential ingredients with reference to Donoghue v. Stevenson and discuss the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Introduction and Definition
Negligence as a tort is the breach of a legal duty to take care which results in undesired damage to the plaintiff. Winfield defines negligence as "the breach of a legal duty to take care which results in damage, undesired by the defendant to the plaintiff."
In Blyth v. Birmingham Waterworks Co. (1856), Alderson, B. defined it as the omission to do something which a reasonable person would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person would not do.

### 2. Essential Ingredients of Negligence
To maintain an action in negligence, the plaintiff must establish three distinct ingredients:

#### A. Legal Duty of Care Owed by Defendant
Negligence cannot exist in the air. The defendant must owe a recognized legal duty of care to the plaintiff.
- Landmark Precedent — Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562:
  Mrs. Donoghue consumed ginger beer manufactured by the defendant, which contained the decomposed remains of a snail. She suffered severe gastroenteritis. Since her friend had purchased the bottle, there was no privity of contract between Donoghue and the manufacturer.
  The House of Lords held that privity of contract was irrelevant to tort liability. Lord Atkin formulated the celebrated "Neighbour Principle":
  "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour... persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation."
- In modern law, the test was refined in Caparo Industries v. Dickman [1990] into a threefold inquiry: (i) Foreseeability, (ii) Proximity, and (iii) Fair, just, and reasonable to impose a duty.

#### B. Breach of Duty
Breach occurs when the defendant fails to adhere to the standard of a reasonable and prudent person. The standard is objective and accounts for:
1. The magnitude and likelihood of risk (Bolton v. Stone).
2. The gravity of potential harm (Paris v. Stepney Borough Council).
3. The cost and burden of precautions (Latimer v. A.E.C. Ltd.).

#### C. Consequential Damage (Not Too Remote)
The plaintiff must have suffered actionable physical, property, or recognized psychiatric damage caused by the breach. Under The Wagon Mound (No. 1) [1961], the damage must be of a type that was reasonably foreseeable by the defendant.

### 3. The Doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur
Normally, the burden of proving negligence rests upon the plaintiff under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly Section 101 of the Evidence Act). However, where the accident speaks for itself, the maxim Res Ipsa Loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") applies.
As laid down in Scott v. London & St. Katherine Docks Co. (1865), three conditions must concur:
1. The instrumentality causing the harm was within the exclusive management and control of the defendant.
2. The accident is such as does not happen in the ordinary course of things without negligence.
3. The true cause of the accident is unexplained by the defendant.

- Application in India:
  In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti (AIR 1966 SC 1750), an 80-year-old clock tower in Chandni Chowk collapsed under normal weather conditions, killing pedestrians. The Supreme Court invoked Res Ipsa Loquitur, holding that clock towers do not collapse without lack of maintenance, shifting the burden to the Corporation, which failed to discharge it.

### 4. Conclusion
Negligence requires duty, breach, and proximate damage. Res Ipsa Loquitur serves as an indispensable evidential aid preventing injustice where the direct proof of carelessness lies solely within the knowledge and control of the tortfeasor.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the evolution of the concept of "Duty of Care" in the law of negligence from Donoghue v. Stevenson to Caparo Industries. Discuss the standards governing professional and medical negligence in India with specific reference to Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Abstract & Introduction
The tort of negligence has evolved from a narrow set of nominate categories into a generalized principle of civil responsibility anchored upon the "duty of care." The concept represents a judicial policy control mechanism determining when one citizen owes legal accountability to another for unintended harm. This answer traces the jurisprudential progression of the duty of care from the "neighbour principle" to the modern tripartite test, and analyzes how Indian courts evaluate professional medical negligence.

### 2. Historical Genesis and the Fallacy of Privity
Prior to 1932, common law courts adhered strictly to the "privity of contract fallacy" (Winterbottom v. Wright, 1842), holding that if a defendant was under a contractual obligation to party A, a third party B injured by the breach could maintain no action in tort.
This barrier was shattered by the House of Lords in Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562. Lord Atkin established that legal duties in tort arise independently of contract. Drawing upon moral jurisprudence, Lord Atkin formulated the universal Neighbour Principle:
"The rule that you are to love your neighbour becomes in law, you must not injure your neighbour... You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour."

### 3. Expansion and Retraction: From Anns to Caparo
#### A. The Expansionary Two-Stage Test (Anns v. Merton LBC [1978])
Lord Wilberforce proposed a broad presumption of duty:
1. Is there a sufficient relationship of proximity or neighbourhood such that carelessness was likely to cause damage?
2. If yes, are there any public policy considerations that ought to negative or reduce the scope of the duty?
This led to an unsustainable expansion of negligence claims, threatening public authorities with indeterminate liability.

#### B. The Modern Pragmatic Tripartite Test (Caparo Industries plc v. Dickman [1990])
The House of Lords decisively retreated from Anns and instituted the current three-stage incremental test:
1. Foreseeability: Was the damage to the plaintiff reasonably foreseeable?
2. Proximity: Was there a relationship of legal proximity between the plaintiff and the defendant?
3. Fair, Just, and Reasonable: Is it fair, just, and reasonable in public policy to impose such a duty on the defendant?
This Caparo framework serves as the touchstone across Commonwealth jurisdictions, balancing compensation for genuine victims against opening floodgates of limitless liability (the specter of liability in an indeterminate amount for an indeterminate time to an indeterminate class, per Cardozo, C.J.).

### 4. Professional and Medical Negligence in India
#### A. The Bolam Test and the Standard of the Professional
When an individual professes a special skill (e.g. medicine, architecture, law), the standard of care is not that of the man on the street.
In Bolam v. Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582, McNair, J. laid down the foundational rule:
"A doctor is not guilty of negligence if he has acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art."
Crucially, a professional is not negligent merely because a contrary body of opinion exists, nor because a higher standard might have averted the outcome.

#### B. Indian Supreme Court Jurisprudence: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) 6 SCC 1
The Supreme Court of India delivered a definitive three-judge bench judgment comprehensively harmonizing civil and criminal medical negligence:
1. Distinction Between Civil and Criminal Negligence:
   - In civil law, negligence is determined on a preponderance of probabilities for breach of reasonable professional competence.
   - For criminal liability under Section 304A IPC (now Section 106 BNS), the negligence must be gross, reckless, or culpable—amounting to an endangerment of human life.
2. Error of Judgment is Not Negligence:
   - A physician cannot guarantee that every patient will be cured or survive surgery. An honest error of judgment in choosing between two recognized therapeutic procedures does not constitute actionable negligence.
3. Procedural Safeguards Established in Jacob Mathew:
   - No criminal complaint against a doctor should be entertained without an independent medical opinion from a qualified government medical expert.
   - Investigating officers should not arrest doctors in a routine manner unless gross negligence is demonstrated.

#### C. Consumer Protection Interplay: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995)
The Supreme Court held that medical services rendered by hospitals and doctors for remuneration fall squarely within the definition of "service" under the Consumer Protection Act. Aggrieved patients can seek speedy, compensatory relief before Consumer Forums for "deficiency of service."

### 5. Remoteness of Damage: The Wagon Mound Principle
Even where duty and breach are established, the defendant is liable only for consequences that are not too remote. In Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. Ltd. (The Wagon Mound No. 1) [1961], the Privy Council overruled the direct consequence rule of In re Polemis [1921], establishing that a tortfeasor is answerable only for the kind or type of damage that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the negligent act.

### 6. Conclusion
The journey of the duty of care reflects the common law's capacity to balance corrective justice with commercial and professional reality. From Donoghue's moral imperative to Caparo's public policy filter, the law guarantees that those who suffer foreseeable injury through careless acts receive restitution, while safeguarding essential professions like medicine through the balanced standards of Bolam and Jacob Mathew.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Scoring Rubric: Allocate 4 marks for historical evolution (Winterbottom, Donoghue neighbour test), 4 marks for Anns to Caparo three-fold test, 5 marks for professional/medical negligence (Bolam, Jacob Mathew guidelines, IMA v. VP Shantha), and 3 marks for remoteness of damage (Polemis vs Wagon Mound) and conclusion.

revisionPoints: Three ingredients: Legal Duty of Care, Breach of Duty (reasonable man test), and Consequential Damage.
Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932): Established independent tort of negligence and Lord Atkin’s Neighbour Principle.
Caparo v. Dickman (1990): Threefold test — Foreseeability, Proximity, and Fair, Just & Reasonable.
Remoteness of Damage: The Wagon Mound (No. 1) [1961] replaced In re Polemis with the test of reasonable foreseeability of kind of harm.
Res Ipsa Loquitur: Rule of evidence shifting the evidential burden to defendant when accident speaks for itself (MCD v. Subhagwanti).
Medical Negligence: Bolam test + Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) — ordinary competence required, gross negligence needed for criminal charges.
examTips: Always cite Donoghue v. Stevenson and quote Lord Atkin’s Neighbour Principle verbatim in university and judiciary mains exams.
Differentiate clearly between civil negligence (remedy: damages) and criminal negligence under BNS s. 106 / IPC 304A (remedy: punishment).
Remember that Res Ipsa Loquitur does not change substantive law; it is an evidential presumption.

enhancement.definition: Negligence is the breach of a legal duty to take reasonable care that causes legally recognised damage.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The claimant ordinarily must establish duty, breach, causation and actionable damage; the standard is objective, subject to context and recognised professional standards.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian tort law is largely uncodified. The governing rules are developed through common-law principles, Indian judicial decisions and applicable legislation for particular fields; no statute should be treated as a general codification of this topic.

- Contributory Negligence: Mitigates damages in proportion to plaintiff's share of responsibility.

Current-law close
In Indian civil practice, plead the specific duty, detail the omission against the reasonable person standard, demonstrate proximate causation under the Wagon Mound test, and claim unliquidated damages calculated on restitutio in integrum.
examples: Example — actionable negligence: A municipal corporation fails to place barricades or warning lights around a deep excavation made in a poorly lit public road. A motorcyclist travelling at a lawful speed falls into the trench and suffers spinal injuries. The corporation owed a duty of care to road users, breached it by failing to fence the hazard, and the physical harm was directly foreseeable. The corporation is liable in negligence.

Example — section/tort not attracted (unforeseeable plaintiff): A railway guard helps a passenger board a moving train. A small, unmarked package wrapped in newspaper drops from the passenger’s arm onto the rails. The package secretly contains fireworks, which explode. The concussive blast knocks down heavy scales thirty feet away, injuring Mrs. Palsgraf. Held: The guard may have been careless to the boarding passenger, but owed no duty of care to Palsgraf because harm to her was completely unforeseeable (Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.).

Example — Res Ipsa Loquitur applied: A pedestrian walking peacefully past a multi-storey flour warehouse is struck on the head by a heavy barrel of flour falling from a second-floor window. The pedestrian cannot prove the precise internal slip by a warehouse worker. Held: Barrels do not roll out of upper windows in the ordinary course of business unless those in control are negligent. The doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur applies, shifting the burden to the warehouse to prove lack of negligence (Byrne v. Boadle).
enhancement.problemApplication: Is Dr. Ananya liable in the tort of negligence? How will the court apply the Bolam test and the Supreme Court guidelines in Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab? — To establish professional medical negligence, the claimant must prove that Dr. Ananya breached the standard of a reasonably competent general surgeon. Under the Bolam test, a medical practitioner is not negligent merely because an alternative course of action or treatment was available, provided the procedure adopted was endorsed by a responsible and respectable body of medical opinion. In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court ruled that a doctor cannot be held liable for an honest error of judgment or an unfortunate surgical complication where ordinary professional competence was applied. Here, Dr. Ananya was confronted with sudden severe vascular adhesions during emergency surgery and adopted a recognized surgical technique. The occurrence of haemorrhage was attributable to unforeseen anatomical fragility rather than gross ignorance, recklessness, or departure from accepted medical practice.
keyTakeaways: Negligence is the breach of a legal duty to take care resulting in damage. Established by proving Duty (Donoghue / Caparo), Breach (reasonable person standard), and Causation (Wagon Mound foreseeability). Supported by Res Ipsa Loquitur and governed in professions by the Bolam / Jacob Mathew standard.

caseLaw.name: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti
caseLaw.holding: The Court applied res ipsa loquitur to the collapse of the clock tower.
caseLaw.relevance: Indian application of res ipsa loquitur.

caseLaw.name: Donoghue v Stevenson
caseLaw.holding: Recognised the neighbour principle in negligence.

caseLaw.name: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman
caseLaw.holding: Set out the foreseeability, proximity and fair-just-reasonable framework in the context of a novel duty of care.

legacyUnverifiedCases.name: Donoghue v. Stevenson
legacyUnverifiedCases.holding: A manufacturer of products sold in such a form as to show that they intend them to reach the ultimate consumer without intermediate examination owes a legal duty of care to the consumer. Formulated the foundational "Neighbour Principle".
legacyUnverifiedCases.relevance: Established negligence as an independent tort and demolished the privity of contract fallacy in product liability.

legacyUnverifiedCases.name: Caparo Industries plc v. Dickman
legacyUnverifiedCases.holding: Formulated the three-fold test for establishing a duty of care in novel situations: (1) foreseeability of harm, (2) proximity of relationship, and (3) that the imposition of liability is fair, just, and reasonable.
legacyUnverifiedCases.relevance: Restricted the over-expansion of negligence liability, particularly for pure economic loss.

legacyUnverifiedCases.name: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
legacyUnverifiedCases.holding: Affirmed the Bolam test for medical negligence in India. Held that an error of judgment or failure to cure does not constitute negligence. For criminal negligence under Section 304A IPC, gross negligence is mandatory.
legacyUnverifiedCases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on medical and professional negligence, shielding doctors from frivolous civil and criminal litigation.

legacyUnverifiedCases.name: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti
legacyUnverifiedCases.holding: The collapse of an 80-year-old clock tower in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, causing deaths of pedestrians, was governed by the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur. The municipal corporation was held liable for failing to maintain and inspect the structure.
legacyUnverifiedCases.relevance: Leading Supreme Court precedent applying Res Ipsa Loquitur to urban infrastructure negligence.
